title: The Covenant with Noah and the Sign of the Bow
summary: God blesses Noah and his sons, renews the command to fill the earth, gives them animals for food but forbids eating blood, and declares that whoever sheds human blood will answer for it because humans are made in God's image. He makes an everlasting covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature never again to destroy the earth by flood, and sets his bow in the clouds as its sign. Later Noah plants a vineyard, becomes drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent; Ham sees and tells his brothers, who cover their father, and Noah curses Ham's son Canaan and blesses Shem and Japheth.
story: The flood is over and the world starts again. Chapter 8 ended with God's private resolve never again to destroy all life; chapter 9 makes that resolve a public covenant. The blessing given to Adam in chapter 1 is repeated to Noah, now adjusted for a world where sin remains: animals will fear humans, meat is permitted, and violence must be restrained by justice. Then the chapter shows how quickly the new start is marred. Noah, the righteous man, is found drunk and exposed, and a family breach opens that will shape the nations. The three sons named here become the subject of the table of nations in chapter 10.
historical:
Ancient treaties between kings often included a sign or witness, and the covenant with Noah follows that pattern with a sign in the sky. The Hebrew word for rainbow is simply qeshet, the ordinary word for a bow, the weapon of war and hunting. Many interpreters have seen a picture of God hanging up his war bow in the clouds after the storm of judgment, although the text itself does not draw that out. What it stresses is that the sign is for God to see and remember, a pledge he binds himself to.

The curse and blessings at the end of the chapter look ahead to peoples Israel knew. Shem is the ancestor of Abraham's family and of other peoples of Mesopotamia and Arabia (chapter 10 and 11:10-26); the modern term Semitic comes from his name. Japheth is linked to peoples to the north and west, including the islands and coastlands of the Mediterranean. Canaan is the ancestor of the peoples who lived in the land promised to Abraham. Israel's later dealings with the Canaanites, including the Gibeonites who became servants at the sanctuary (Joshua 9:23), form the background against which Israel heard Noah's words.
cultural:
The ban on eating meat with its blood rests on a conviction that ran through Israel's law: life belongs to God, and blood represents life (Leviticus 17:11). Humans may take animal life for food, but they must drain the blood and so acknowledge that life is God's gift and not theirs to consume. Later rabbinic tradition spoke of commandments given to all the descendants of Noah, including this one and the ban on murder, as God's law for every nation. The early church, deciding what to ask of Gentile believers, included abstaining from blood (Acts 15:20).

In an honor-based culture, a father's dignity was closely guarded, and exposing or mocking a parent was a grave offense. Shem and Japheth take great care not to see their father, walking backward with a garment on their shoulders. Ham's act, whatever exactly it was, disgraced his father in front of the family. Curses and blessings spoken by a dying or aged father were taken to shape the future of the children who received them, a belief that will surface again with Isaac and Jacob.
literary: The chapter has three parts. Verses 1 to 7 are framed by the command to be fruitful and multiply, which opens and closes the section and deliberately echoes 1:28. Verses 8 to 17 are dominated by one word, covenant, which appears seven times, and by the repeated phrase every living creature; the effect is slow, solemn, and emphatic, like a legal document read aloud. Verses 18 to 29 return to narrative and form a sad echo of Genesis 3. A man of the soil plants something, eats or drinks its fruit, and ends up naked and shamed; covering follows, and a curse is spoken. The difference is that here the cursed party is a grandson. The chapter closes with the familiar genealogical refrain from chapter 5 (and then he died), marking the end of Noah's story.

outline.t: The blessing renewed, the gift of meat, and the value of human life
God's covenant with every living creature
The bow in the clouds as the covenant sign
Noah's drunkenness and his sons' response
Canaan cursed, Shem and Japheth blessed

doctrines.note: God's covenant with Noah is made with all humanity and every living creature, and it depends on God alone. Noah is not asked to do anything to keep it in force. It guarantees the stability of the world in which God's later covenants with Abraham, Israel, and David will unfold, and the prophets appeal to it as a model of God's faithfulness (Isaiah 54:9-10).

Even after the flood, and even with sin still in the human heart, every person bears the image of God. That is why murder is so grave: to strike a human being is to strike God's image. Verse 6 grounds the sanctity of human life not in a person's usefulness or innocence but in God's creation.

God gives rules for the new world: respect for life shown in not eating blood, and accountability for bloodshed. Many Christian interpreters have seen here the foundation of human justice and government, the authority given to people to restrain violence. Others read verse 6 as a description of how violence returns on the violent. Either way, bloodshed is not left unanswered.

The new world has barely begun before sin shows itself in its best man. Noah's drunkenness and Ham's dishonoring of him make clear that the flood washed away a generation, not the sin in the human heart. The story shows sin spreading from one generation to the next.

words.note: Qeshet, bow. It is the everyday word for the archer's bow, used here for the rainbow. Some have seen in it God's war bow laid aside after judgment. The key point is that God sets it in the clouds as a sign for himself: whenever it appears, he will remember his covenant.

Dam, blood. In the Old Testament blood stands for life, and shed blood for violent death. Verses 4 to 6 use it both ways: the blood of animals must not be eaten because it is their life, and human blood must not be shed because humans bear God's image. Blood will become central to Israel's sacrifices.

Darash, to seek, inquire, or require, translated require and demand an accounting in verse 5. The same verb is used for seeking God in prayer and for God investigating wrongdoing. Here it means God will hold every killer, human or animal, to account for a human life.

Ervah, nakedness or exposure. It often carries a sense of shame, and the phrase to uncover nakedness is used in Leviticus 18 as a euphemism for forbidden sexual relations. That usage lies behind some interpretations of Ham's act. In this chapter, at minimum, it names the disgrace of Noah's exposure, which Shem and Japheth cover.

christ: The covenant with Noah does not name a Savior, but it sets the stage on which God's saving work unfolds. By promising to preserve the world and every living creature, God keeps open the time in which his purposes for all nations can be fulfilled. The rainbow reappears in the Bible's visions of God's glory: Ezekiel sees the brilliance around God's throne as like that of a rainbow in a cloud (Ezekiel 1:28), and John sees that “a rainbow that gleamed like an emerald encircled the throne” (Revelation 4:3). The sign of God's mercy after judgment surrounds the throne of the one who rules history. The chapter's teaching on blood also runs forward. Israel learned that life is in the blood and that blood makes atonement (Leviticus 17:11), and Jesus spoke of his death as “My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). These are thematic links that the New Testament develops, not predictions in Genesis 9.

hard.q: Why is Canaan cursed for what Ham did, and was this passage used to justify slavery?
hard.a:
The text is difficult in several ways. It does not say exactly what Ham did. The plain reading is that he looked on his father's shame and made it known, dishonoring him. Others, noting that uncovering a father's nakedness is a sexual euphemism in Leviticus 18, suggest a more serious act. Nor does the text explain why Noah curses Canaan rather than Ham. Some suggest a punishment fitting the crime, a son who dishonored his father being punished through his own son; others think Canaan was somehow involved; others read Noah's words as a prophecy pointing forward to the Canaanites' later conduct and history, with which Israel's first readers were familiar. It should also be noticed that the curse comes from Noah, not from God.

This passage was badly misused for centuries. From the medieval period onward, and especially in the defense of slavery in the Americas in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, some Christians claimed that Africans descended from Ham and bore a divine curse of servitude. The text does not support this. The curse falls on Canaan, not on Ham or his other sons, and the Canaanites lived in the land of Canaan, not in Africa. The use of Genesis 9 to justify racial slavery is now recognized across Christian traditions as a serious misreading that served human cruelty. Genesis itself grounds the dignity of every person in the image of God, three verses earlier in the same chapter.

questions: God grounds the value of human life in his own image, not in what a person can do. How might that change the way you treat people others consider unimportant?
God sets the rainbow as a sign for himself, to remember his promise. What does it mean to you that God binds himself to keep his word?
Shem and Japheth covered their father's shame instead of exposing it. When someone close to you fails, how do you decide between covering a fault and addressing it?
